title: X.509 Internet Public Key Infrastructure Online Certificate Status Protocol - OCSP
summary: This document specifies the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP), a way to find out the current status of a digital certificate without Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs). It obsoletes RFCs 2560 and 6277 and updates RFC 5912.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of reading a long list of cancelled IDs, you ask a server "is this ID still good?" and get a quick answer.

questions: how to check certificate revocation status online
what does revoked mean in ocsp
subtitle: How a program asks a server, in real time, whether a digital certificate has been revoked.

tldr.problem: Checking a certificate against a periodically published revocation list can be too slow when timely information is needed, for example for high-value funds transfers or large stock trades.
tldr.mechanism: An OCSP client sends a status request naming the certificate to an OCSP responder, which returns a signed response saying good, revoked or unknown, together with a validity interval.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6960 obsoletes RFC 2560 and RFC 6277, and has itself since been updated by RFC 8954 and RFC 9654.

today: RFC 6960 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2560 and RFC 6277 and updates RFC 5912. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8954 and RFC 9654.

sections.title: Why OCSP Exists
sections.content:
The Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) determines the current status of a digital certificate without requiring Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs). The RFC says that in lieu of, or as a supplement to, checking a periodic CRL, it may be necessary to get timely revocation information, and gives examples such as high-value funds transfers or large stock trades.

RFC 6960 replaces RFC 2560 and RFC 6277. Its main reason for being is to fix ambiguities found since RFC 2560. The changes include allowing the revoked answer for certificates that were never issued, clarifying when a responder counts as an Authorized Responder, adding the missing ASN.1 syntax for the nonce extension, and adding the preferred signature algorithms extension from RFC 6277.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates are like ID cards that can get cancelled. OCSP lets you ask whether one card has been cancelled, instead of checking a huge list.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Certificate Status
sections.content:
An OCSP client sends a status request to an OCSP responder and suspends acceptance of the certificates in question until the responder answers. A request carries a protocol version, the service request, the target certificate identifier and optional extensions. The responder checks that the message is well formed, that it is configured to provide the service, and that the request has the information it needs. If not, it returns an error message; otherwise it returns a definitive response.

Every definitive response MUST be signed and carries one of three statuses for each certificate:

  • good: at a minimum, no certificate with that serial number currently within its validity interval is revoked. It does not necessarily mean the certificate was ever issued.
  • revoked: the certificate has been revoked, temporarily (reason certificateHold) or permanently. It MAY also be returned for a serial number the CA has no record of issuing.
  • unknown: the responder does not know the certificate, usually because it does not serve that issuer. The client may then try another source such as a CRL.

For a non-issued certificate answered with revoked, the responder MUST include the extended revoked definition extension, use reason certificateHold (6) and set the revocation time to January 1, 1970.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is one of three: "yes, it is fine", "no, it was cancelled" or "I do not know that one". The office signs every real answer so you know it is genuine.

sections.title: Request and Response Messages
sections.content:
The messages are defined in ASN.1 and signed data is encoded with DER. A request (OCSPRequest) holds a tbsRequest and an optional signature. Each single request names its target with a CertID: a hash algorithm, a hash of the issuer's distinguished name, a hash of the issuer's public key, and the certificate serial number. The key hash is included because two CAs may use the same name but will never share a public key unless they deliberately share a private key or one key was compromised. A requestor MAY sign the request, and if it does it SHALL give its name in requestorName.

A response (OCSPResponse) has a responseStatus and, on success, responseBytes. The basic response type (id-pkix-ocsp-basic) MUST be supported by every responder and client. It contains the responder ID, a producedAt time, one SingleResponse per certificate, optional extensions and a signature. The response MUST include a SingleResponse for each certificate in the request and SHOULD NOT include extras, although pre-generating responders might.

Four times matter: thisUpdate (when the status was known to be correct), nextUpdate (when newer information will be available), producedAt (when the responder signed) and revocationTime. Responses whose nextUpdate is earlier than local time, or whose thisUpdate is later, SHOULD be considered unreliable.
sections.plainLanguage: The question names the card by who issued it and its number. The answer lists the card, its status and a time stamp saying how fresh the answer is.

sections.title: Who May Sign a Response
sections.content:
A response key MUST belong to the CA that issued the certificate, a Trusted Responder whose public key the requestor trusts, or a CA Designated Responder (Authorized Responder). The key that signs status information need not be the key that signed the certificate, but the signer must be authorized.

A CA delegates by issuing the responder a certificate whose extended key usage contains id-kp-OCSPSigning. That certificate MUST be issued directly by the CA named in the request, and the CA SHOULD use the same issuing key it used for the certificate being checked. A client MUST reject a response unless the signing certificate matches a local configuration, is the issuing CA's own certificate, or carries id-kp-OCSPSigning and was issued by that CA.

Before accepting a signed response a client SHALL confirm that the certificate matches the request, the signature is valid, the signer is the intended recipient and currently authorized, thisUpdate is recent enough, and (when present) nextUpdate is later than the current time.

Since a delegated responder's own certificate could be revoked, the CA can include the id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck extension to say the responder is trusted for the life of its certificate, point to a revocation checking method, or leave it to the client's local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the card office, or someone the office has given a special signed note to, may answer. Your checker looks for that note before trusting the answer.

sections.title: Error Responses
sections.content:
When something goes wrong, the responder returns an error message that is not signed. The defined errors are malformedRequest (the request does not conform to OCSP syntax), internalError (the responder reached an inconsistent state, so retry, perhaps with another responder), tryLater (the service exists but is temporarily unable to respond), sigRequired (the server requires a signed request) and unauthorized (the client is not authorized to ask, or the server cannot answer authoritatively).

Because errors are unsigned, the Security Considerations warn that an attacker could send false error responses.
sections.plainLanguage: If the office is confused or busy it says so, for example "try again later". These notes are not signed, so they are less trustworthy than real answers.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
Support for all extensions is optional for clients and responders, and the critical flag SHOULD NOT be set on them. Unrecognized extensions MUST be ignored unless they are marked critical and not understood. The RFC defines these:

  • Nonce: binds a request to its response to prevent replay attacks.
  • CRL References: tells which CRL a revoked certificate was found on, by URL, CRL number or time.
  • Acceptable Response Types: lists the response types a client can accept.
  • Archive Cutoff: the producedAt time minus the responder's retention interval, useful for showing a signature was reliable when made, even if its certificate has expired.
  • Service Locator: lets a server route a request to the server authoritative for the certificate.
  • Preferred Signature Algorithms: lets a client list, most preferred first, the algorithms it wants the response signed with. The responder SHOULD apply the lowest-numbered of five listed selection mechanisms that gives a supported, strong enough algorithm.
  • Extended Revoked Definition: signals that the responder answers revoked for non-issued certificates.

Clients SHALL be able to process responses signed with RSA with SHA-256, and SHOULD also handle RSA with SHA-1 and DSA with SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions are optional extras on the form, such as a secret number that proves the answer matches your question, or a note about which signing style you prefer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
OCSP only helps if certificate-using systems can reach the status service. If they cannot, they could fall back to CRL processing.

The RFC lists several weaknesses. A flood of queries is a denial-of-service risk, and signing each response makes it worse. Precomputed responses allow replay of an old good response after the certificate has been revoked but before it expires, so deployers should weigh that benefit against the risk. Requests do not name the responder they are for, so an attacker can replay a request to many responders. Misconfigured HTTP caches can give unexpected results.

Answering revoked for a never-issued certificate could let someone get a revocation response for a serial number that will soon be issued, if it can be guessed. The specification handles this by requiring certificateHold, and CAs can avoid it entirely with random, high-entropy serial numbers.

The preferred algorithms mechanism is not protected against a man-in-the-middle downgrade. The RFC accepts this because the responder MUST NOT sign with weak algorithms even if asked, and the client can reject responses that do not meet its criteria.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might flood the office with questions or replay an old "it is fine" answer. The rules tell offices to be careful about both.

sections.title: OCSP over HTTP
sections.content:
Appendix A describes carrying OCSP over HTTP. Requests can use GET or POST. Small requests (less than 255 bytes after encoding) MAY use GET so that HTTP caching works; otherwise, or when caching does not matter, the request SHOULD use POST. For GET the DER request is base-64 encoded and URL-encoded and appended to the URL. For POST the Content-Type is application/ocsp-request and the body is the DER request.

The response uses Content-Type: application/ocsp-response with the DER OCSPResponse as the body. Where privacy is required, the exchange MAY be protected with TLS/SSL. The responder's location normally comes from the authority information access extension in the certificate, which CAs SHALL be able to include and which carries the id-ad-ocsp access method and a URI.
sections.plainLanguage: On the web, you can send your question as a short link or as a small package, and the answer comes back labelled as an OCSP answer.

messages.label: OCSPRequest
messages.note: Names the target certificate by issuer name hash, issuer key hash and serial number.

messages.label: OCSPResponse
messages.note: Signed status (good, revoked or unknown) with a validity interval, or an unsigned error.
